segments.text: Welcome to the presentation of filter.
In this SO paper, we uncover security
and functional gaps in AI based fishing
website detection literature.
My name is Mahabu Alalom and this is
joint work with my co-authors at Texas&M
and California State University San
Marcos.
Fishing detection papers report really
high accuracy
obtain over 98%.
But fishing is the most reported cyber
crime to the FBI.
191,000 incidents last year
and it's a gateway to major cyber crimes
like ransomware and databases.
Total cyber crime losses reached $20.9
billion in 2025.
The problem is that benchmark accuracy
doesn't tell us how these detectors
actually perform in the real world.
To understand the gap between benchmark
accuracy and real world performance, we
distilled four functionality and three
security requirements
and then developed a code book defining
high, medium and low fulfillment
criteria for each.
On the functionality side, we have
fishing tactic diversity, benign page
diversity interpretability
and evaluation transparency.
Attackers use many fishing tactics.
Some impersonate popular brands like
Facebook or Amazon.
Others impersonate an organization's
internal portal or regional sites.
Some hide behind trusted shared hosting
domains
and some even put a capture in front so
fishing content onlyly appears after you
solve it.
The problem is a method that works well
against a fake Amazon page may fail
completely on a fake HR portal.
So with fishing tactic diversity, we ask
two things.
Does the paper clearly scope which
tactics its method can detect?
And does it report a performance
breakdown for each tactic it claims to
handle.
Similarly, we check if it is tested for
false positives on diverse benign pages.
Does it explain its decisions
and does it report metrics that account
for class imbalance?
On the security side, the key challenge
is that fishing is not static.
Attackers constantly change their
techniques.
New fishing kits, new page designs, new
brands to impersonate.
So a detector that performs well today
may quietly degrade over time. We assess
whether the method account for this
evolution.
We also ask can it resist adversarial
and evasion attacks and does it protect
user privacy.
We followed Prisma guidelines to select
a representative set of fishing website
detection papers.
We searched in DBLP using the query
combining fishing with URL or P terms
and with detection or attack terms.
That gave us an initial corpus of 288
papers from 178 venues.
Then we performed abstract and full text
screening to keep only the papers with
AI based detection methods.
This process left us with 55 papers in
the final corpus.
Then we categorized the selected papers
into four groups by detection strategy.
Feature based, similarity based,
identity based and hybrid.
Feature based methods they train a
machine learning classifier using
features extracted from the URL or the
page.
Similarity based methods on the other
hand compare visual or structural
similarity with a set of reference
sites.
And if they find uh like using this
method they identify whether the
page under
evaluation is actually mimicking a
reference legitimate site
and identity based methods. They infer
whose brand or organization the page
claims to be using the logo or the text
in the page and the design and then
check whether the domain actually belong
to that brand.
and hybrid methods they combine two or
more of this approach.
